name: Investigate incidents and audit field safety
summary: This process deals with every worker injury, near miss, vehicle incident, property damage and electrical contact at a city-owned electricity distributor, and with the planned field audits that safety advisors make of line and cable crews. A crew supervisor reports the incident, the on-call safety advisor opens a case and decides which legal notices are due (Ministry of Labour, joint health and safety committee and union, WSIB), then the supervisor and advisor investigate at the site, write the causes and corrective actions, and the safety manager signs off. Field audits check a crew's permits, PPE, cover-up and approach distances on the job. Work is slow mainly because field supervisors write reports between crew jobs, cases wait for the monthly committee meeting, and corrective actions wait for training seats and crew time.

baseline.org_archetype: A municipally owned Ontario electricity distributor of about 570 staff and 346,000 customers, with unionised line, cable and station crews and a seven-person health, safety and environment team.
baseline.notes: Incidents are recorded in a health and safety incident system; reports, photos and notices move by email. The safety management system was certified to OHSAS 18001 and moved to ISO 45001 in 2021 (ho_ar2021). Pandemic precautions in 2020-2022 added COVID-19 case tracking, which is outside this workflow.

unit_of_work: one incident or one field safety audit
trigger: A supervisor reports an injury, near miss, vehicle incident, property damage or electrical contact, or a planned field audit comes due on the monthly audit plan.
end_state: The investigation report is approved, corrective actions are verified and the case is closed, or the audit is recorded with any findings closed.

volume.seasonality: More incidents and audits from May to October, when construction, pole replacement and vegetation work peak; fewer in January and February. Cold-weather slips and vehicle incidents rise in winter.

evidence.note: Organisation file range kept. An all injury/illness frequency rate of 1.17 in 2021 (ho_cir2021), read as per 200,000 hours worked, means about 6 to 7 recordable injuries a year for about 570 staff; the rest of the about 230 incident cases a year are first aid cases, near misses, vehicle and property damage incidents (author's estimate), plus about 16 field audits a month.

surge.cause: major storm restoration with long crew shifts

evidence.note: Organisation file assumption of one to four declared major events a year (May 2022 derecho as the large case). More vehicle, fatigue and near-miss incidents during restoration while planned audits stop; the multiplier is the author's estimate.

Organisation file role (6 advisors, on call). Advisors also run environment, training support, PPE and JHSC programs, so about 1.6 FTE of the 6 goes to incident investigation and field audits. Loaded cost from the organisation file (wage x 1.40).
Organisation file role (1). Approves investigation reports, makes Ministry notices for critical injuries and chairs reviews; about 15 percent of the manager's time.

Organisation file role (8 overhead supervisors). Supervisors lead investigations of incidents on their crews and close corrective actions. The supervisor steps also stand for underground and stations supervisors when the incident is on their crews.

Organisation file role (4). Does the same supervisor steps as the overhead supervisor for cable crews; the steps are written with the lines-supervisor role, so this FTE is not driven by any step in the simulation.

Organisation file role (62). Crew members attend the debrief at the end of a field audit (four people for about 15 minutes) and give witness statements; their witness time is inside the supervisor interview step.
Organisation file role (8). Assumed to handle WSIB Form 7 filing and claim management in HR's disability management function; in some utilities the safety advisor files it instead.
Organisation file role (3). Reviews the few incidents that point to a design, material or work method problem.

systems.name: Health, safety and environment incident system
Mobile workforce management and field tablets
Time entry for crews and staff
Document management and engineering drawing repository

resources.name: Light vehicle (pickup or van) for locators, meter technicians, inspectors and field service
Overhead line crew (three to four line trades with a bucket truck and a digger)

steps.name: Receive report or audit assignment and open case
steps.description: The on-call safety advisor takes the supervisor's phone call or the initial incident e-form, or picks up the next planned field audit from the monthly audit schedule. They open a case in the health and safety incident system with date, crew, location, type (injury, near miss, vehicle, property damage, electrical contact, or audit) and a short description.

error.defect_description: Incident type or severity recorded wrongly at first call.

evidence.note: Incident and audit share is the author's estimate for a utility of about 570 staff: about 19 incidents and 16 audits a month. Advisors are on call, so most reports are opened within the hour; e-forms sent at night wait for the morning.

steps.name: Classify severity and decide the notices required
steps.description: The advisor checks the injury against the critical injury definition and the WSIB health care and lost time tests, and checks whether a member of the public or utility plant was involved. They decide which notices are due (Ministry of Labour, JHSC and union, WSIB) and whether the case also goes to the distribution safety compliance team.

error.defect_description: A reportable injury is classed as first aid only, so the WSIB or JHSC notice is late.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act ss. 51-52 and Workplace Safety and Insurance Act reporting duties

next.condition: injury needing health care or lost time
near miss, first aid, vehicle or property damage

evidence.note: Notice categories from the OHSA guide and the WSIB page. Shares are the author's estimate: an all injury/illness frequency rate of 1.17 in 2021 (ho_cir2021), read as recordable injuries per 200,000 hours, gives about 6 to 7 recordable injuries a year for about 1.1 million hours, so about 4 percent of about 230 incident cases a year; critical injuries are taken as under one a year.

steps.name: Notify the Ministry, JHSC and union and send the written report
steps.description: For a death or critical injury the safety manager phones the Ministry's Health and Safety Contact Centre, the JHSC worker co-chair and the union immediately, makes sure the scene is held, and within 48 hours sends the written report with the prescribed particulars to a Ministry Director.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 51(1): immediate notice of death or critical injury and written report within 48 hours

evidence.note: Immediate notice and written report within 48 hours under s. 51(1) of the OHSA, as stated in the Ministry guide.

steps.name: File the WSIB employer's report of injury
steps.description: The HR advisor collects the injury details from the case and the supervisor, enters the Form 7 on the WSIB online service with wage and return-to-work information, and starts the claim file. Late filing brings a WSIB penalty.

error.defect_description: Wage or date details wrong on the Form 7.

control.basis: Workplace Safety and Insurance Act: employer's report within three business days

evidence.note: Three business days after the reporting obligation begins (wsib_report). Who files it (HR) and the touch time are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Send the written injury notice to the JHSC and union
steps.description: The advisor writes the notice with the prescribed particulars of the injury and sends it to the JHSC co-chairs and the union steward. The notice is copied into the case file.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 52(1): written notice to JHSC and union within four days

evidence.note: Written notice within four days for an injury needing medical attention or causing disability from usual work, s. 52(1) of the OHSA.

steps.name: Travel to the incident site or service centre
steps.description: The advisor drives a utility light vehicle to the incident site while the conditions can still be seen, or to the service centre where the crew and vehicle are, often the next working day.

evidence.note: Ottawa service territory of about 1,116 square kilometres; 20 to 70 minutes each way is the author's estimate. Most investigations start the same or next working day.

steps.name: Inspect the scene and collect evidence
steps.description: The advisor photographs the site, equipment, vehicle damage or tool involved, measures distances and checks the cover-up, grounding and traffic set-up against the work protection permit and the pre-job briefing form. They take copies of the permit, the briefing form and any statements.

evidence.note: Evidence steps follow the usual incident investigation method of ISO 45001-certified utilities (ho_ar2021 confirms the certification, not the steps); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Interview the crew and witnesses
steps.description: While the advisor examines the scene, the crew's supervisor interviews the injured or involved worker, the crew lead and other witnesses one at a time, and writes down the sequence of events and what was different from the plan.

error.defect_description: Statements miss a contributing factor, such as a change of plan not briefed to the whole crew.

evidence.note: Supervisor-led investigation with advisor support is the author's description of common utility practice; times are estimates.

steps.name: Pull system records for the incident
steps.description: Back at the office the advisor pulls the switching and outage records, vehicle telematics for vehicle incidents, the worker's training and qualification records and the crew's job record, and attaches them to the case.

evidence.note: Records consulted are the author's estimate from the organisation file's systems.

steps.name: Analyse root causes and draft the investigation report
steps.description: The supervisor writes the investigation report in the incident system: sequence of events, immediate and root causes, and corrective actions with owners and dates. Field supervisors fit this between crew work, so reports often wait several days.

error.defect_description: Root cause stops at 'worker error' or the corrective actions do not match the causes.

evidence.note: Report drafting by the supervisor and a one-week typical delay are the author's estimate; utilities commonly set an internal target of five to ten working days.

steps.name: Review the report and corrective actions
steps.description: The advisor checks that the causes are supported by the evidence, that each cause has an action, and that the actions go beyond retraining where a hazard can be removed. Weak reports go back to the supervisor with comments.

evidence.note: Return rate is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve the report and decide escalation
steps.description: The safety manager reads the report, signs it off and decides whether the case goes further: to the standards engineer when equipment or a work method is involved, to the enterprise risk register when serious, and to training when retraining is needed.

control.basis: Company health and safety management system (ISO 45001-certified) incident investigation procedure: management review and sign-off

next.condition: equipment, material or work method involved

evidence.note: Manager sign-off is the author's description of a certified management system's incident procedure; share referred to standards is an estimate.

steps.name: Review the equipment or work method involved
steps.description: The standards engineer checks the construction standard, approved material or work method named in the report, compares it with the manufacturer data and industry practice, and decides whether to issue a standard change or a safety bulletin.

evidence.note: Link from incidents to standards maintenance is in the organisation file's process map; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Table the case at the joint health and safety committee
steps.description: The advisor adds the case to the next joint health and safety committee meeting package with the causes and actions, presents it, and records the committee's questions or recommendations in the case.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 9: joint health and safety committee to be informed and to make recommendations

evidence.note: The committee must meet at least every three months (on_jhsc); a monthly meeting at a utility is the author's estimate, so cases wait up to a month. Corrective work starts before the meeting, which is why the next step's wait is short.

steps.name: Complete the corrective actions
steps.description: The supervisor arranges the actions: a crew tailboard on the lessons, a tool or equipment repair, a change to the job plan template or a training refresher booked with the training coordinator. They mark each action done in the incident system.

evidence.note: Waits for training seats, tools and crew time are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Verify the actions and close the case
steps.description: The advisor checks evidence that each action is done (sign-in sheet, repair record, revised form) and closes the case, or reopens an action that was not done.

next.condition: action not done or no evidence

evidence.note: Verification before closure is common in certified management systems; reopen rate is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Pick a crew and job to audit
steps.description: The advisor looks at the next days' crew schedule in the mobile workforce system and picks a crew and job type that is due for an audit under the audit plan, such as live-line work, pole setting, cable splicing or traffic control.

evidence.note: Advisors working through a monthly field audit plan is the author's estimate of common practice; the number of audits (about 16 a month across six advisors) is an estimate.

steps.name: Drive to the crew's job site
steps.description: The advisor drives a utility light vehicle to the work site. Audits are put off when a storm pulls crews onto restoration or the job is rescheduled for weather.

evidence.note: Travel time and weather delays are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Observe the crew's work against the audit checklist
steps.description: The advisor watches the job without stopping it and checks the pre-job briefing form, work protection permit, PPE and rubber gloves, cover-up, grounding, minimum approach distances, traffic control and housekeeping, ticking each item on the field audit checklist. They stop the work only for an imminent hazard.

error.defect_description: An unsafe practice is missed because the crew changed behaviour while observed.

control.basis: Company field safety audit program under the occupational health and safety management system

evidence.note: Checklist items reflect common utility work rules (work protection, approach distances); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Debrief the crew on what was seen
steps.description: At a natural break the advisor and the crew talk through the good practices and the gaps seen, agree on fixes that can be made on the spot, and the crew lead signs the checklist. The whole crew stops work for the talk.

evidence.note: A four-person crew (the organisation file's overhead crew of three to four trades) stops for 10 to 30 minutes; author's estimate.

steps.name: Enter the audit results in the incident system
steps.description: Back at the office the advisor types the checklist results and photos into the health and safety system, scores the audit and flags findings that need a corrective action from the supervisor.

error.defect_description: Finding entered against the wrong crew or supervisor.

evidence.note: Share of audits with findings needing follow-up is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assign and complete the corrective action
steps.description: The supervisor gets the audit finding by email from the system, agrees the fix (a tool replaced, a crew refresher, a missing permit field corrected) and records when it is done.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Confirm the audit action is closed
steps.description: The advisor checks the supervisor's evidence that the fix is in place and closes the audit record, so it counts in the monthly safety report to management.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Critical injury
exceptions.description: A worker is critically injured. The scene is held for the Ministry inspector, the safety manager makes the immediate and 48-hour notices, a JHSC worker member joins the investigation, and the WSIB report and JHSC notice follow.

exceptions.name: Injury with health care or lost time
exceptions.description: The WSIB Form 7 and the written JHSC and union notice are due within three business days and four days before the investigation is finished.

exceptions.name: Weak investigation report returned
exceptions.description: The advisor sends the report back because the causes stop at worker error or the actions do not match the causes.

exceptions.name: Standards or work method review
exceptions.description: An incident points to a construction standard, approved material or work method, so the standards engineer reviews it before closure.

exceptions.name: Corrective action not done at verification
exceptions.description: The advisor finds no evidence that an action is done and sends it back to the supervisor.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from report or audit assignment to case closed
benchmarks.population: All incident and audit cases at a mid-size Ontario distributor, 2019-2022

evidence.note: No published figure found. Author's estimate: audits close within about a week, incidents within three to eight weeks once corrective actions are done; with 45 percent audits the median case is about two weeks.

benchmarks.unit: injuries and illnesses per 200,000 hours worked (unit assumed)

evidence.note: Value as reported; the report does not state the hours basis.

benchmarks.unit: lost workdays per 200,000 hours worked (unit assumed)

evidence.note: Value as reported; the report does not state the hours basis.

benchmarks.unit: hours per trades employee per year

evidence.note: 15 hours averaged across all employees.

pain_points.description: Field supervisors draft investigation reports between crew jobs and storm call-outs, so reports wait about a week and then often come back for weak root causes.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from common utility practice.

pain_points.description: Cases wait for the next joint health and safety committee meeting and corrective actions wait for training seats and crew time, which stretches closure to weeks.

evidence.note: Committee meeting rule from on_jhsc; the delay itself is the author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Evidence sits in several systems (outage records, telematics, training records, permits on paper or tablets), so the advisor spends an hour or more assembling it for each case.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from the organisation file's systems list.

pain_points.description: Storms stop planned field audits and add fatigue and vehicle incidents, so the audit plan falls behind in summer.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

sources.supports: Custom scorecard safety measures for 2021: All Injury/Illness Frequency Rate 1.17 and Lost Workday Severity Rate 3.11, both with a target of 'reduce'.

sources.title: Hydro Ottawa Holding Inc. 2021 Annual Report
sources.supports: Integrated health, safety and environment management system moved from OHSAS 18001 to ISO 45001 and ISO 14001 certification in 2021; safe work practices training averaged 15 hours per employee and 44 hours for trades employees; safety performance described as on par with industry peers.

sources.title: Guide to the Occupational Health and Safety Act: Part VII Notices
sources.publisher: Government of Ontario, Ministry of Labour, Immigration, Training and Skills Development
sources.supports: For a death or critical injury the employer notifies the Ministry (Health and Safety Contact Centre), the joint health and safety committee and the union immediately and sends a written report to a Ministry Director within 48 hours (s. 51(1)); for an injury needing medical attention or causing disability from usual work, written notice to the committee and the union within four days (s. 52(1)), and to the Ministry if an inspector requires it.

sources.title: Guide for health and safety committees and representatives
sources.publisher: Government of Ontario, Ministry of Labour, Immigration, Training and Skills Development
sources.supports: A designated worker member of the joint health and safety committee inspects the workplace at least once a month; the committee meets at least once every three months (s. 9(33)); worker members designate one or more members to investigate a death or critical injury (s. 9(31)).

sources.title: Report a workplace injury or illness (employers)
sources.supports: The employer's accident report (Form 7) must reach the WSIB within three business days after the reporting obligation begins; reporting is needed when the worker needs health care beyond first aid, loses time or pay, or does modified work beyond seven days.

assumptions: The process mixes two kinds of case: incidents (about 55 percent) and planned field audits (about 45 percent). Both start at the same intake step so that one file covers the process map entry.

Supervisor steps are written with the overhead lines supervisor role; underground and stations supervisors do the same work for their crews, and their time is stated as FTE on the roles list rather than as separate steps.

The joint health and safety committee wait (up to a month) is on the critical path because cases are closed only after the committee has seen them; corrective work starts in parallel, so the corrective action step's wait is short.
WSIB Form 7 filing is placed with HR's disability management function; some utilities give it to the safety team instead.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's (wage x 1.40). Labour cost per case leaves out the time of the injured worker and of the external parties (Ministry inspector, WSIB).
Ministry of Labour inspector visits and orders after a critical injury are outside this workflow; they add weeks to the few cases they touch.

Simulated median cycle time (about 24 days over all cases) is 1.6 times the author's benchmark of 15 days. Split by case type the simulation gives incidents a median of about 33 days (p90 about 44) and audits about 7 days (p90 about 18), both inside the ranges the benchmark rests on; the gap comes from the benchmark's rough guess at how the two types mix, so the step times were left as they are. No published cycle time for utility incident investigations was found.
